title: Cleaning and saving water: why mud sinks, and how to waste less

summary.text: Muddy water holds tiny bits of clay that can float for a day or more, even though clay is heavier than water. A pinch of phitkari, called alum in English, makes those bits stick together into clumps that sink in minutes. City water plants clear river water the same way, then pass it through sand and add a little chlorine to kill germs. Clear water is not always safe, so drinking water still needs boiling or a good purifier. Clean water takes a lot of work to make, so it is worth saving. A home saves water by turning taps off, fixing leaks and using kitchen water again for plants and mopping.
summary.art: Two glasses of muddy water side by side: one still cloudy brown, the other clear with a layer of brown mud at the bottom and a small white phitkari crystal next to it. Behind them, a girl pours rice-washing water from a bowl into a potted tulsi plant.

intro.hook: Stir a spoon of soil into a glass of water and leave it on the table. The sand sinks in seconds. But the water above it can stay cloudy all day. Clay is heavier than water, so why doesn't it sink?
intro.text: Barbers and grandmothers across India keep a white crystal called phitkari, or padikaram in Tamil. In this unit you rub a little of it in muddy water and watch what happens to the cloudiness. You find out why the tiniest bits of dirt stay up, and how cities clean river water for millions of homes. Then you look at your own home and find where clean water is lost, and how to use it twice.
intro.art: A child's hand holding a glass of cloudy brown water up to a window, with a few grains of sand already lying at the bottom.

outcomes: I can explain why big bits of dirt sink fast and the tiniest clay bits stay floating for a long time.
I can run a fair test to show what phitkari does to muddy water, and record how clear it gets over time.
I can say the main steps a city uses to clean water: clumping, settling, sand filtering and adding chlorine.
I can explain why clear water is not always safe to drink, and what makes it safe.
I can measure how much water different ways of washing use, and pick the way that wastes least.
I can sort used water by where it can go next: plants, mopping, flushing or the drain.
I can tell how Hamburg and Altona showed in 1892 that filtering water through sand stops cholera.

terms.meaning: Water with tiny bits of soil, sand or clay floating in it, which make it cloudy.
terms.example: After heavy rain, the water in a river or a new puddle looks brown and muddy.
terms.art: A glass of brown, cloudy water.

terms.meaning: To sink slowly to the bottom of still water.
terms.example: Leave a bucket of muddy water still, and sand settles to the bottom in a few seconds.
terms.art: A bucket of water with a layer of sand at the bottom and clearer water above.

terms.meaning: Soil made of the very smallest bits, far too small to see one at a time. Wet clay is sticky.
terms.example: Red soil and multani mitti are full of clay. They make water cloudy for a long time.
terms.art: A lump of sticky red clay in a child's hand.

terms.meaning: A white crystal that makes tiny bits in water stick together. Its English name is alum. In Tamil it is padikaram.
terms.example: Barbers rub phitkari on the face after a shave. Families have used it for hundreds of years to clear well and river water.
terms.art: A clear-white lump of phitkari crystal on a steel plate.

terms.meaning: A soft clump of tiny dirt bits that have stuck together in water. Flocs are big enough to sink.
terms.example: Rub phitkari in muddy water and, after a few minutes, you see little fluffy flocs drifting down.
terms.art: Fluffy brown clumps drifting down through water in a glass.

terms.meaning: Making tiny bits in water stick together into clumps. Phitkari does this.
terms.example: A water treatment plant adds alum to river water. This coagulation makes the mud clump so it can settle out.
terms.art: Tiny dots in water joining into bigger clumps, with arrows.

terms.meaning: Something with small gaps that lets water through but catches bits that are too big for the gaps.
terms.example: A tea strainer is a filter for tea leaves. A cotton cloth is a finer filter.
terms.art: Muddy water poured through a cloth tied over a steel tumbler.

terms.meaning: A deep layer of sand that water trickles down through. Dirt is caught in the tiny gaps between the grains.
terms.example: Many cities pass their water through beds of sand as big as a room before it goes into pipes.
terms.art: A cut view of a tank with water on top of a thick sand layer and gravel underneath.

terms.meaning: Living beings far too small to see, such as bacteria and viruses. Some of them make people ill.
terms.example: Cholera is caused by a germ that lives in dirty water.
terms.art: A magnifying glass over a drop of water, showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: A chemical added in very small amounts to drinking water to kill germs.
terms.example: City water sometimes smells a little like a swimming pool. That is the chlorine.
terms.art: A water treatment worker adding a measured dose to a big tank.

terms.meaning: To make water safe to drink by killing or removing the germs and harmful things in it.
terms.example: Boiling water for one minute purifies it of germs.
terms.art: A steel vessel of water boiling on a stove, with steam rising.

terms.meaning: To use something carefully so that it lasts, and not waste it.
terms.example: Turning off the tap while you brush your teeth conserves water.
terms.art: A child turning off a tap while holding a toothbrush.

terms.meaning: To use something again for another job.
terms.example: Water used to wash rice can water a potted plant.

terms.meaning: Water that has been used and is now dirty, such as water from a bath, a sink or a toilet.
terms.example: Waste water from your flat runs down the drain pipe to a sewer.

explanations.concept: Why big bits sink fast and tiny bits stay up
explanations.definition: In still water, a bit of dirt that is heavier than water sinks. But the smaller the bit, the more slowly it sinks. The tiniest clay bits sink so slowly that they can stay floating for a day or more.
explanations.description: When something sinks, the water has to move out of its way, and that slows it down. A big sand grain is heavy for its size and pushes through quickly. A clay bit is so tiny that the water slows it almost to a stop. If a sand grain were as small as a clay bit, it would sink just as slowly. So size matters as much as what the bit is made of. That is why muddy water first drops its sand, then its silt, and keeps its clay floating.
examples: A shaken bottle of soil and water shows layers within a minute: small stones at the bottom, sand above them, then fine silt. The water on top stays cloudy.
Dust in a sunbeam floats in the air for a long time, though dust is heavier than air. It is the same idea: tiny bits fall very slowly.
After the monsoon, a lake can stay brown for weeks, because the fine clay is still floating in it.
explanations.art: A tall glass of water with three layers at the bottom (pebbles, sand, silt) and cloudy water above, with tiny dots labelled clay.
explanations.context: This card explains why some dirt sinks in seconds and some stays floating for days. It is about what you saw in the shaken bottle.

explanations.concept: Why clay bits don't clump by themselves
explanations.definition: Each tiny clay bit carries a small electric charge on its surface. All the bits carry the same kind of charge, so they push each other away. They keep apart and never grow big enough to sink.
explanations.description: You can feel this kind of push with two balloons rubbed on your hair. They push each other away, because they carry the same kind of charge. Clay bits in water do the same thing on a tiny scale. Even when two bits drift close, they push apart again. So the water stays cloudy for a long time.
examples: Two balloons rubbed on your hair and hung side by side swing away from each other.
Multani mitti stirred into water can keep it cloudy for days.
explanations.art: Tiny clay bits drawn as dots, each with a small minus sign, with little arrows showing them pushing each other apart.
explanations.context: This card explains why the tiny clay bits in muddy water stay apart instead of sticking together and sinking.

explanations.definition: Phitkari, or alum, dissolves in water. It cancels the charges on the clay bits and forms a sticky jelly that catches them. The bits stick together into flocs. Flocs are big enough to sink. This is called coagulation.
explanations.description: Rub a lump of phitkari in muddy water for a few seconds and wait. After a few minutes, you see small fluffy clumps. These are flocs. They grow and drift down. Within about half an hour, much of the mud lies on the bottom and the water above is clearer. Nothing has been taken away. The same clay is still in the glass, joined into fewer, bigger clumps. Too much phitkari makes the water sour and is not good to drink, so people use only a little.
examples: In many Indian villages, people rub a lump of phitkari around the inside of a water pot, then wait for the mud to settle.
Water treatment plants in Indian cities add alum, or a similar chemical, to river water as the first cleaning step.
In a glass of muddy water with phitkari, the flocs look like tiny bits of brown cotton wool.
explanations.art: Three glasses in a row: cloudy water, then small fluffy flocs forming, then clear water with mud on the bottom. A phitkari lump beside the first.
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Phitkari Test, where muddy water with phitkari cleared and plain muddy water did not.

explanations.concept: How a sand filter cleans water
explanations.definition: A sand filter is a deep layer of sand that water trickles down through. The gaps between the sand grains are tiny. Bits of dirt get stuck in the gaps or cling to the grains.
explanations.description: Water takes a twisting path through millions of tiny gaps. Many small bits get caught on the way. In a slow sand filter, a thin layer forms on top of the sand. It is full of tiny living beings, such as bacteria and other microbes. They eat many of the germs in the water. Engineers call this layer by its German name, schmutzdecke, which means 'dirt cover'. So the slimy top of the filter does much of the cleaning. Every few weeks, workers scrape off the top layer, and the living layer grows again.
examples: James Simpson built a large slow sand filter for a water company in London in 1829.
Under a river bank, river water seeps through sand and gravel. Wells dug near rivers often give clearer water than the river itself.
explanations.art: A cut view of a sand filter: dirty water on top, a thin green-brown living layer on the sand, thick sand, gravel underneath, and clear water flowing out of a pipe at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains how sand can clean water, and the living layer on top that does much of the work.

explanations.concept: How a city cleans its water
explanations.definition: A city water plant cleans river or lake water in steps. First it adds alum or a similar chemical so the mud clumps. Next the water sits still in big tanks so the clumps settle. Then it trickles through sand filters. Last, a little chlorine is added to kill germs that are left.
explanations.description: Each step catches what the step before missed. Clumping and settling take out most of the mud. The sand catches smaller bits. Chlorine kills germs that are too small for the sand to catch. A little chlorine stays in the water, so it keeps killing germs on the long trip through the pipes. Then the water is pumped to tanks and pipes across the city. Bengaluru's water comes from the Kaveri river, about 100 kilometres away, and has to be pumped uphill to reach the city. All that work is why clean tap water is precious.
examples: Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Kochi and other cities each run large water treatment plants.
A faint swimming-pool smell from the tap means a little chlorine is still working in the water.
explanations.art: A simple left-to-right picture of a water plant: a river, a mixing tank with alum, a settling tank, a sand filter bed, a chlorine tank, and a pipe going to a city of flats.
explanations.context: This card follows river water through the steps a city uses to make it clean.

explanations.concept: Clear is not the same as safe
explanations.definition: Clumping, settling and filtering make water clear. But germs are far too small to see, and many can pass through cloth or a home sand filter. To make water safe to drink, it must also be purified.
explanations.description: Water that looks clear can still hold germs, and things dissolved in it, like salt. After using phitkari or a filter, families boil drinking water for at least one minute, or use a purifier that kills germs. Clearing first still helps, because boiling and purifiers work better on clear water. In this unit, never drink the water from any test.
examples: A glass of clear well water can carry germs that cause diarrhoea.
Boiling water for one minute kills the germs that cause cholera and typhoid.
explanations.art: Two glasses of clear water side by side: one with a magnifying circle showing tiny germs, the other steaming from a boiled vessel.
explanations.context: This card explains why water that looks clean still needs boiling or a purifier before you drink it.

explanations.concept: Old ways of clearing water in India
explanations.definition: Long before machines, people in India cleared muddy water with phitkari and with seeds. The kataka seed, called thetran kottai in Tamil and nirmali in Hindi, is rubbed inside a wet clay pot. It makes the mud clump and settle, like phitkari does.
explanations.description: Old Ayurvedic books, such as the Sushruta Samhita, name the kataka seed as a way to clear water. In parts of South India some families still use it. In Sudan, in Africa, women cleared Nile river water with crushed seeds of the moringa tree. That is the same drumstick tree whose pods go into sambar. In the 1970s and 1980s, a German scientist, Samia Al Azharia Jahn, studied how the Sudanese women did it. Scientists now test moringa seeds as a low-cost way to clear water.
examples: A clay pot with a kataka seed rubbed on its inside wall.
Dried drumstick seeds, crushed into a powder and stirred into muddy water.
explanations.art: An old clay pot on a kitchen floor, a hand rubbing a small round seed on its inner wall, and a few drumstick pods lying beside it.
explanations.context: This card is about how people in India and Africa cleared water with seeds long before water plants were built.

explanations.concept: Is alum in drinking water safe?
explanations.description: Water plants use alum, and a tiny amount of aluminium can stay in tap water. Most health scientists say the small amounts in properly treated water are safe. Some people still worry, and scientists keep checking. Everyone agrees that using too much alum is wrong, and that plants must measure their dose carefully.
examples: The World Health Organization gives a guide value for how much aluminium treated water should have, and water plants test for it.
At home, people rub only a little phitkari and let the water settle before using it.

perspectives.explanation: The small amount of aluminium in well-treated water is safe. We take in far more aluminium from food than from water.

perspectives.who: Some scientists and many worried people
perspectives.explanation: In the 1980s, a few studies suggested aluminium might be linked to memory illness in old age. Later studies did not show that clearly. They want plants to keep the amount as low as possible.

explanations.art: A scientist in a lab holding up a small glass of treated water against a light, with a chart on the wall.
explanations.context: This card is about a real question people ask: is the alum used to clear water safe?

explanations.concept: Where water is lost at home
explanations.definition: Most water wasted at home goes down the drain without doing any job. It runs while nobody is using it, leaks from taps and toilets, or overflows from tanks.
explanations.description: A running tap pours out many litres every minute. If it runs while you scrub a plate or brush your teeth, most of that water does nothing. A small leak in a flush or a tap runs all day and all night. Many building tanks overflow when the motor is left on. The water you wait through for the hot water to come is clean too. Much of this water can be saved by turning taps off, fixing leaks and catching water in a bucket.
examples: Scrape leftover food into the bin before washing a plate, so you need less water to rinse it.
Catch the cold water from the shower or the geyser pipe in a bucket while you wait for hot water. Use it for the toilet or the mop.
A plastic bottle filled with water and put in an old large toilet tank makes each flush use less.
explanations.art: A cartoon home cut open: a running tap with nobody near it, a dripping flush, an overflowing tank on the roof, each with a small blue arrow going down a drain.
explanations.context: This card shows where a home wastes clean water without anyone noticing.

explanations.definition: Grey water is water that has been lightly used, such as water from washing vegetables, rinsing rice, washing hands or bathing. It can be used again for jobs that don't need clean water.
explanations.description: Water from washing rice, dal or vegetables is good for plants. Soapy bath or hand-washing water can be used for flushing the toilet or mopping. Water with a lot of oil, food or strong cleaners should go down the drain. Toilet water is never reused at home, because it carries germs. Some buildings in Bengaluru and Chennai now clean their grey water in small plants and use it for gardens and flushing.
examples: Rice-washing water poured into the tulsi pot.
The last rinse water from the washing machine, caught in a bucket and used to wash the balcony.
explanations.art: Arrows from a kitchen sink and a bathroom bucket to a potted plant, a mop and a toilet, with a red cross on an arrow from an oily kadai.
explanations.context: This card is about which used water can do a second job, and which must go down the drain.

explanations.concept: Why home RO purifiers throw water away
explanations.definition: An RO purifier pushes water through a very fine sheet that lets water through but holds back salts and germs. The salts left behind are washed away with some of the water. This is called reject water.
explanations.description: RO stands for reverse osmosis. Many home RO purifiers send away two or more litres of reject water for each litre of drinking water, though newer ones waste less. Reject water is salty, so it is not good for plants every day. It is fine for mopping, washing vehicles or flushing the toilet. If your tap water is not salty, a purifier that kills germs without RO may be enough. A water test tells you which you need.
examples: Many families put a bucket under the RO's reject pipe and use the water for mopping.
Some RO machines show how much water they have purified, so you can compare it with the reject bucket.
explanations.art: A wall-mounted water purifier with two pipes: one filling a steel jug with drinking water, the other filling a bucket with reject water.
explanations.context: This card explains why many home water purifiers send water away, and how to use that water.

explanations.concept: Why save water if the Earth has so much?
explanations.definition: About 97 out of every 100 litres of water on Earth is salty sea water. Most of the fresh water is frozen in ice or deep underground. Only a small part is in rivers, lakes and the ground near the surface, where people can easily use it.
explanations.description: Water is not used up. It goes round and round in the water cycle. But clean fresh water, in the right place at the right time, is limited. Cities spend a lot of energy cleaning and pumping it. In India, most fresh water goes to farming, so the food we eat carries a lot of water too. Saving water at home matters, and so does wasting less food.
examples: Chennai ran very short of water in 2019, when its lakes nearly dried up.
Growing rice takes a lot of water, so throwing away a plate of rice also throws away water.
explanations.art: 100 drops in a grid: 97 blue for sea water, 2 white for ice, 1 bright blue for the water we can use.
explanations.context: This card explains why fresh clean water is limited, even though the Earth looks like a blue planet.

agreed.text: Tiny bits of clay stay floating for a long time because they are so small, and because their same charges keep them apart.
agreed.evidence: Settling speeds have been measured in labs for over a hundred years. Anyone can watch muddy clay water stay cloudy for a day.

agreed.text: Alum makes tiny bits in water clump and settle.
agreed.evidence: Water engineers test this every day in 'jar tests', where they add different amounts of alum to jars of river water and watch them clear.

agreed.text: Filtering through sand removes much of the dirt and many germs from water.
agreed.evidence: Cities with slow sand filters, like Altona in 1892, had far less cholera than cities drinking the same river water unfiltered.

agreed.text: Water must be boiled, chlorinated or purified to be safe to drink, even when it looks clear.
agreed.evidence: Germs are too small to see. Tests on clear water often find germs, and boiling or chlorine kills them.

agreed.text: Turning off taps, fixing leaks and reusing grey water save a large share of the water a home uses.
agreed.evidence: Families who measure their water before and after these changes see their use fall.

challenging.claim: If water looks clear, it is clean and safe to drink.
challenging.for: Muddy water often does make people ill, and clear water often does not.
challenging.against: Germs and dissolved salts or chemicals are invisible. Clear water can carry cholera. Only purifying makes it safe.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common mistake: thinking clear water is always safe.

challenging.claim: Heavy things always sink fast, so if dirt is still floating, it must be lighter than water.
challenging.for: Big stones sink fast and leaves float.
challenging.against: Clay is heavier than water, yet its tiny bits float for a day or more. Size slows sinking. Clumped, the same clay sinks in minutes.
challenging.context: This card tests a common guess about why things sink or float in water.

challenging.claim: Saving a bucket of water at home makes no difference, because farms use most of the water.
challenging.who: Some people, when asked to save water
challenging.for: In India, most fresh water does go to farming.
challenging.against: City water is cleaned and pumped at great cost, and it is short in summer. A family saving 50 litres a day saves over 18,000 litres a year. Many families together save a lot.
challenging.context: This card is about whether saving water at home really matters.

challenging.claim: Every home needs an RO purifier.
challenging.for: RO removes salts and germs, and some tap water in India is salty or has harmful salts.
challenging.against: Where water is not salty, a purifier that kills germs, or boiling, is enough. RO also throws away a lot of water and some useful minerals.
challenging.context: This card is about whether every home needs an RO water purifier.

challenging.claim: Cholera spreads through bad air from rotting rubbish.
challenging.who: The 'miasma' idea, held by many doctors until the late 1800s
challenging.for: Cholera was worst in smelly, crowded places.
challenging.against: Smelly places also had the dirtiest water. In 1892, Altona's filtered water kept cholera low next to Hamburg, with the same air.
challenging.context: This card is about an old wrong idea of how cholera spreads.

big_questions.q: Clay is heavier than water. So is a tiny clay bit floating, or is it falling very, very slowly?
big_questions.hint: Watch a glass of muddy water for a whole day. Does the cloudy part get lower?

big_questions.q: Phitkari did not take any mud out of the glass. Yet the water became clearer. Where did the cloudiness go?
big_questions.hint: Look at the bottom of the glass. Is the same mud still there?

big_questions.q: Sand filters work because tiny living beings eat the germs. Who else is cleaning the water you drink, without you knowing?
big_questions.hint: Think of the soil, the sand under a river, and the living beings in them.

big_questions.q: Who should pay for clean water: every family, the city, or nobody?
big_questions.hint: Think about the work and the energy it takes to clean and pump water to your flat.
What is the water itself, and what is carried in it?

big_questions.q: If you save a bucket of water today, where does that water go instead?
big_questions.hint: It stays in the tank, the lake or the ground. Who else can use it?

story.title: The Brown Tap
story.note: Phitkari (padikaram) and the kataka seed (thetran kottai) are really used to clear water in South India, and clear water really still needs boiling. Meenakshi, her family and this flat in Madurai are made up.
text: It was the hottest week of May in Madurai. The Vaigai river was almost dry, and the corporation water came only every second morning.
Meenakshi was in Class 3. She lived on the third floor with her Appa, her Amma and her grandmother, Kamala Paati.
On Tuesday the water came at six in the morning, as it always did. But this time it came out of the tap brown.
Appa held up a steel tumbler of it. 'Look at this! It's like filter coffee.'
The watchman called up from below. 'A big pipe burst on the main road. They mended it last night. Mud got in.'
Appa frowned. 'The whole tank on the terrace is full of this now. We'll have to empty it down the drain and call a tanker.'
Amma shook her head. 'A tanker costs a lot in May. And who knows when the next one will come?'
Meenakshi looked at the tumbler. Tiny brown specks were spinning slowly in the water. A few grains of sand had already dropped to the bottom. The rest of the water stayed brown.
Kamala Paati came out of the kitchen with her old tin box. 'Before we pour away a whole tank of water,' she said, 'let me try something.'
She opened the box. Inside was a lump of white crystal, like a piece of frosted glass.
'Padikaram!' said Meenakshi. 'The barber uses that after a shave.'

'Yes,' said Paati. 'And in my village, near the river, we used it every day. River water came brown after the rains. My mother rubbed padikaram inside the pot, or a thetran kottai seed, and the mud went down.'
Appa laughed. 'Amma, that's an old village trick. This is city water.'
Meenakshi had an idea. 'Let's test it, Appa. Two tumblers of the same brown water. Padikaram in one, nothing in the other.'

She filled two steel tumblers right to the top. Paati held the crystal and swirled it in the first tumbler, ten slow times round. Then she lifted it out. Meenakshi stirred the second tumbler ten times with a spoon, so that both had the same stirring.
'Now nobody touches them,' said Paati.
They sat on the floor and watched. For a few minutes, nothing seemed to happen. Then Meenakshi bent close to the first tumbler.
'Paati, there are little fluffy things in it! Like tiny bits of brown cotton.'
The fluffy bits grew bigger and began to drift down, like slow brown snow. Appa put down his phone and came to look.
After half an hour, the first tumbler had a soft brown layer at the bottom. The water above it was clear enough to see the steel shining through. The second tumbler was still brown all the way down.
'But both had the same mud,' said Appa. 'Why did one sink and not the other?'
Meenakshi thought about it. 'The mud bits were too tiny to sink on their own. They just kept floating. The padikaram made them stick together into clumps. Clumps are big, so they sink.'
'So the mud is still there,' said Appa slowly. 'It's just sitting at the bottom now.'
'Yes,' said Paati. 'Nothing has gone. It has only gathered.'
That afternoon, Appa and Meenakshi filled every bucket in the house from the tank. Paati swirled the padikaram in each one. By evening, every bucket had clear water on top and mud at the bottom.
Appa dipped a tumbler into the clear water. 'Now we can drink it.'
'No, Appa!' said Meenakshi. 'Clear is not the same as clean. Germs are too small to see. The pipe was broken, so germs could have got in too.'
Paati nodded. 'Clear water is ready for boiling. It is not ready for drinking.'
So Amma boiled the drinking water, and let it cool in the clay pot. They used the clear bucket water for cooking, bathing and washing.
At the end, there were only a few cups of thick mud left at the bottom of the buckets. Meenakshi did not pour them down the drain. She stirred them into the soil of the jasmine pot on the balcony.
Appa watched her. 'Only one small bowl of mud. We nearly threw away the whole tank because of that.'
Two days later, the water came clear again. But Appa kept a lump of padikaram on the kitchen shelf, just in case.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the mud in the tank was made mostly of tiny clay bits. They were heavier than water, but so small that they sank too slowly to see. Their same electric charges also kept them apart. Padikaram, which is alum, cancels those charges and makes the bits stick together into fluffy clumps called flocs. The flocs are big enough to sink, so the water above clears. No mud was removed: it only gathered at the bottom. Because germs may have got in through the broken pipe, the clear water still had to be boiled before drinking. By clearing the water instead of throwing it away, the family saved a whole tank.
ask: Why did the sand drop to the bottom of the tumbler straight away, but the brown colour stayed?
Why did Meenakshi stir the second tumbler ten times too?
What were the fluffy brown things Meenakshi saw?
Why did Meenakshi stop Appa from drinking the clear water?
Paati knew this from her village, and Appa thought it was only an old trick. How did the family find out who was right?

Nobody switched off the motor. The terrace tank overflowed. Lose 5 drops.
You washed vegetables in a bowl, not under a running tap. Gain 2 drops.
The RO reject water went down the drain. Lose 2 drops. Say one job it could have done.
You used the RO reject water to mop the floor. Gain 2 drops.
You turned off the tap while soaping your hands. Gain 1 drop.
A tap is dripping in the bathroom. Lose 2 drops, unless you tighten it now.
You covered the plant pots with dry leaves, so they need less watering. Gain 2 drops.
QUESTION: Why does clay stay floating in water? Right answer: gain 2 drops. (Its bits are so tiny that they sink very slowly, and their charges keep them apart.)
QUESTION: What does phitkari do to muddy water? Right answer: gain 2 drops. (It makes the tiny bits clump into flocs, which sink.)
QUESTION: Is clear water always safe to drink? Right answer: gain 2 drops. (No. It may still have germs. Boil it or purify it.)
QUESTION: Name one thing a city adds to kill germs in water. Right answer: gain 2 drops. (Chlorine.)
QUESTION: Which used water can go to plants: rice-washing water or oily kadai water? Right answer: gain 2 drops. (Rice-washing water.)
QUESTION: What is the living layer on top of a sand filter good for? Right answer: gain 2 drops. (Its tiny living beings eat germs.)
TEST IT: Hold your hands under the tap for 10 seconds into a mug. How full is the mug? Everyone who guessed within a finger's height gains 1 drop.
TEST IT: Count how many mugs fill a bucket. Gain 1 drop for doing it.

printables.title: 30 paper water drops for each player, and one counter each

rules: Each player starts with 10 drops and a counter on START.
On your turn, roll the dice and move. On a KITCHEN, BATHROOM, BALCONY or TANK square, take the top card and do what it says.
On a plain square, nothing happens.
QUESTION cards: another player reads it and checks the answer in brackets. Playing alone, answer out loud, then read the brackets.
When you pass START, the week begins again. Gain 3 drops from the city supply.
If you run out of drops, your family must wait for a tanker: miss one turn, then start again with 5 drops.
After everyone has gone round twice, the player with the most drops wins. Playing alone, try to finish two rounds with more than 20 drops.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the board. 2. Give each player 10 drops and a counter on START. 3. Shuffle the cards face down.
flow.say: Each drop is a bucket of clean water for our family's week. Some things save water and some waste it. Let's see who keeps the most.
flow.kid: Put your counter on START. Take 10 drops. Mix up the cards. Can you keep your family's water?
flow.context: This is the first step of Every Drop Counts. It is a board game about saving water in a flat. Here you set up the board.

flow.do: Play the card 'The tap ran while you brushed your teeth' as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. The tap ran while you brushed your teeth. What could you do instead?
flow.kid: Practice card. The tap ran while you brushed. What could you do instead?

check.q: The tap ran while you brushed your teeth. What saves the most water?
options: Brush faster with the tap running
Wet the brush, turn the tap off, then rinse with one mug
check.why: Turning the tap off while you brush stops the water that does no job. One mug is enough to rinse. Brushing faster still lets clean water run down the drain while you brush.

flow.do: Play two rounds. Read each card out loud. When a QUESTION card comes, let the player answer before reading the brackets.
flow.say: Before you read the answer in brackets, tell me why you think so.
flow.kid: Roll and move. Read the card out loud. Say your answer before you look at the brackets.
flow.parent: If a child is losing many drops, ask: 'What could that family do next time?' The game is about noticing choices, not about luck.

ask.q: Which cards saved the most drops?

flow.do: Count the drops. Then ask your child to choose one card that could really happen in your home this week.
flow.say: Which card could happen in our home? What will we do about it?
flow.kid: Count your drops. Pick one card that could happen at home. What will you do?
flow.think: Which way of losing water in the game do you think wastes the most in a real home?

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the board and give each player 10 drops.

setup.caption: 2. Land on a room, take a card and gain or lose drops.

games.title: Which Water Where? A sorting card game
games.context: This card game is about grey water. Players match cards of used water to the job each can do next: plants, mopping, flushing, or the drain.

printables.title: 12 used-water cards
items: Last rinse water from the washing machine
Oily water from washing the kadai
Cold water caught while waiting for the geyser
Water left in your bottle from yesterday

printables.title: Answer key for the parent
items: Plants: rice water, vegetable water, egg water, yesterday's bottle water, cold geyser water
Mopping: RO reject water, machine rinse water, cold geyser water
Flushing: bath water, hand-washing water, mopping water, machine rinse water
Only the drain: oily kadai water, toilet water

rules: Lay the 4 job cards face up in a row.
Shuffle the used-water cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take a card, read it out loud, and put it under the job you think it can do. Say why.
If another player disagrees, both give a reason. Then check the answer key.
Score 1 point for a match the key agrees with. Some cards fit more than one job: any job on the key scores.
Playing alone, sort all 12, then check the key and count your points.

flow.do: Lay out the 4 job cards. Shuffle the used-water cards.
flow.say: Every card is water that has already been used once. Your job is to find a second job for it, if it can have one.
flow.kid: Lay out the 4 job cards. Each water card needs a second job. Or the drain.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Water Where. It is a sorting game about using water twice.

flow.do: Take turns to sort the cards. Ask for a reason each time.
flow.say: Where does this water go? Why can't it go to the plants?
flow.kid: Read your card. Put it under a job. Say why.

check.q: Ammu, a girl in Class 3 in Kochi, has a bowl of oily water from washing the kadai. Where should it go?
check.why: Oil coats the soil and the roots, so plants can't take in water and air well. Oil also leaves the floor greasy. So oily water goes down the drain. Rice and vegetable water are the best for plants.

flow.parent: Soapy water is fine for flushing and mopping. A little mild soap water now and then does not harm most plants, but it is better not to use it every day.

flow.do: Check the answer key together. Talk about any card you disagreed on.
flow.say: Which card was hardest to sort? Why?
flow.kid: Check the key. Which card was hardest? Why?

ask.q: Why can RO reject water mop a floor but not water plants every day?
good: Salt builds up in the soil

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the 4 job cards.

experiments.title: The Phitkari Test: can a crystal clear muddy water?
experiments.question: Two glasses hold the same muddy water. If we rub phitkari in one and not the other, will one clear faster?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will rub phitkari in one glass of muddy water and only stir the other. Which glass will be clearer after 30 minutes? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both glasses get the same water, the same amount of soil and the same stirring. Only the phitkari changes. That way, any difference must come from the phitkari.
results_table: Glass A, no phitkari: can you read the letters?
Glass A: height of clear water on top (cm)
Glass B, with phitkari: can you read the letters?
Glass B: height of clear water on top (cm)

materials.item: two tall clear glasses or clear plastic bottles cut in half, the same size
2 spoons of red soil or soil from a plant pot, or 1 spoon of multani mitti
a small lump of phitkari, about the size of a peanut, or a small pinch of phitkari powder
a spoon for stirring, a ruler and a clock
a sheet of paper with a big word written in thick black marker

experiments.safety: Nobody drinks any of the test water. Phitkari is safe to touch, but wash your hands after, and keep it away from eyes and mouths.

schedule.what: Make the muddy water, add phitkari to one glass, and look at both after 5 minutes.
Look again at 15 and 30 minutes, and once more later in the day. Fill in the table and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at 0, 5, 15 and 30 minutes, and once more 2 hours later. Draw both glasses at 30 minutes, showing the clear part and the mud.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make two glasses of the same muddy water. You rub phitkari in one, and watch what happens to the cloudiness in each.

flow.do: 1. Fill a jug with 2 glasses of tap water. 2. Stir in the soil or multani mitti for one whole minute. 3. Pour half into each glass. 4. Label them A and B.
flow.say: We are making one batch of muddy water, then splitting it. That way both glasses start exactly the same.
flow.kid: Stir the soil into the jug for a whole minute. Pour half into each glass. Call them A and B.
flow.parent: Potting mix that is mostly cocopeat floats and makes brown water that phitkari clears less well. Red soil, garden soil or multani mitti gives the best cloudy water, because they are full of clay. Multani mitti is sold cheaply at most grocery and medical shops.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Phitkari Test. You make one batch of muddy water and split it into two glasses.

flow.do: 1. Hold the paper with the big word behind each glass. 2. Can your child read the word through the water? 3. Write 'no' or 'yes' for both glasses at 0 minutes.
flow.say: Can you read the word through the water? This is how we will measure how clear each glass is.
flow.kid: Hold the paper behind each glass. Can you read the word? Write yes or no.

ask.q: Why do we look at the word through both glasses, and not just say which looks clearer?
good: So we measure the same way each time

flow.do: Ask your child for a guess and a reason before adding the phitkari. Write the guess down.
flow.say: I will rub phitkari in glass B. I will only stir glass A. Which will be clearer in 30 minutes? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess! Which glass will be clearer in 30 minutes? Why? Write it down.

flow.do: 1. Hold the phitkari lump and swirl it in glass B, round and round, for 10 seconds. Lift it out. 2. Stir glass A for 10 seconds with a clean spoon. 3. Put both glasses side by side and don't touch them again.
flow.say: Glass A gets the same stirring as glass B. So if B clears faster, it can only be because of the phitkari.
flow.kid: Swirl the phitkari in glass B for 10 seconds. Stir glass A for 10 seconds too. Now don't touch them!
flow.parent: If you only have powder, stir a small pinch, held between finger and thumb, into glass B instead. More is not needed.

flow.do: After 5 minutes, look closely at glass B from the side, near a window.
flow.say: Look very closely at glass B. Can you see anything new in the water?
flow.kid: Look closely at glass B. What can you see in the water now?
flow.parent: Small fluffy clumps, called flocs, usually appear within a few minutes and start drifting down. Glass A looks the same as at the start. If nothing happens in B after 10 minutes, rub the phitkari for another 10 seconds.

flow.do: At 15 and at 30 minutes: 1. Do the word test on both glasses. 2. Measure the height of the clear water on top with a ruler. 3. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Let's read the word again, and measure how much clear water is on top of each glass.
flow.kid: Read the word through each glass. Measure the clear water on top. Write it in the table.

check.q: At 30 minutes, glass B has mud on the bottom and clear water on top. Glass A is still cloudy. What made the difference?
options: The phitkari made the tiny mud bits stick into clumps that sank
Glass B had less mud in it
check.why: Both glasses had the same mud and the same stirring. Only the phitkari was different. It made the tiny clay bits stick together into flocs, and the flocs were heavy enough to sink. Picking 'less mud' is a natural thought, but the mud is all still there, lying on the bottom.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: phitkari makes muddy water clear. What I saw: in glass B, fluffy clumps formed and sank, and I could read the word after 30 minutes. Glass A was still too cloudy. Why: the phitkari made the tiny mud bits stick together, and big clumps sink. Look at glass A again 2 hours later, or before bed. It is often still cloudy.
flow.think: The mud in glass B is all still there, on the bottom. So what really changed?

setup.caption: 2. Swirl phitkari in B. Stir A the same amount.

experiments.title: The Plate Test: which way of washing wastes least water?
experiments.question: Three ways of washing the same dirty plate: under a running tap, scrub first with the tap off, or scrape first and dip in a bowl. Which uses least water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which way will use the least water, and which the most? About how many mugs will each use? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three plates of the same kind with the same amount of the same food, dried for the same time. Wash each until it squeaks clean. Catch every drop in a basin and measure it with the same mug.

materials.item: 3 steel plates of the same size
3 spoons of the same leftover food, such as curd rice or dal
a big basin or bucket that fits in the sink, to catch the water
a mug, a scraper or spoon, a small bowl, dish soap and a scrubber

experiments.safety: Do it at the kitchen sink. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Wash three plates in three ways, catch all the water, and measure it in mugs.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each way of washing, one square for each mug.
experiments.context: In this experiment you wash three plates with the same food on them in three different ways, catch all the water, and measure which way uses least.

flow.do: 1. Spread one spoon of the same food on each plate. 2. Leave them for 10 minutes so the food dries a little. 3. Put the basin in the sink.
flow.say: All three plates get the same food and the same drying time. So the only thing that changes is how we wash them.
flow.kid: Put one spoon of food on each plate. Wait 10 minutes. Put the basin in the sink.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plate Test. You make three plates equally dirty before washing them three ways.

flow.do: Ask for a guess for each way, in mugs, and a reason. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: How many mugs do you think each way will use? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how many mugs each way will use. Why? Write it down.

flow.do: Way 1: Hold plate 1 under the running tap. Scrub it with soap until clean, with the tap on all the time. Then measure the water in the basin by scooping it out with the mug.
flow.say: Way 1: the tap stays on the whole time. Let's count every mug.
flow.kid: Way 1. Keep the tap on while you scrub. Then scoop out the basin with the mug. Count the mugs.
flow.parent: Help your child keep the tap at the flow your family usually uses. Pour the measured water into a bucket to mop with or flush, so the test water is not wasted.

flow.do: Way 2: Wet plate 2, turn the tap off, scrub with soap, then turn the tap on only to rinse. Measure the water.
flow.say: Way 2: the tap is off while we scrub.
flow.kid: Way 2. Wet the plate. Tap off. Scrub. Tap on only to rinse. Count the mugs.

flow.do: Way 3: Scrape plate 3 into the bin first. Dip it in a small bowl of water and scrub with soap. Rinse it with one mug of water poured slowly. Measure everything, counting the bowl too.
flow.say: Way 3: scrape first, then wash in a bowl, then rinse with one mug.
flow.kid: Way 3. Scrape the food into the bin. Wash in a bowl. Rinse with one mug. Count it all.

flow.do: Compare the three numbers. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which way used least water? Were all three plates clean? Why did that way use less?
flow.kid: Which way used least? Were all the plates clean? Why?

check.q: Lakshmi, a girl in Mysuru, washed plates in all three ways. Way 1 used 8 mugs, way 2 used 4 and way 3 used 2. Why did way 1 use the most?
options: The tap ran the whole time, even while she scrubbed
check.why: While she scrubbed, the water ran straight down the drain without doing any job. Ways 2 and 3 only used water when it was needed. Scraping first meant there was less food to wash away.

flow.parent: In most homes, way 1 uses several times as much as way 3, but your numbers depend on your tap. Any result is a real result. If two ways come out the same, try them once more, because one try can be a fluke.

experiments.title: The Leaf Blanket: does covering the soil save water?
experiments.question: If we cover the soil in a pot with dry leaves, does it stay wet longer than bare soil?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Two pots of wet soil sit in the sun. One has a blanket of dry leaves on top. Which will dry out first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two pots or steel tumblers of the same size, filled with the same soil and the same amount of water, in the same sunny spot. Only the leaf cover changes.
results_table: Bare pot: top feels wet or dry?
Covered pot: top feels wet or dry?

materials.item: 2 small pots, cups or old steel tumblers of the same size
soil to fill both
a mug of water
a handful of dry leaves, or shredded newspaper, or dry coconut husk
a sunny windowsill or balcony

experiments.safety: Wash your hands after touching soil.

schedule.what: Fill both pots with the same soil, water them the same, and cover one with dry leaves. Put both in the sun.
Feel the top of both, then push a finger 2 cm down. Is it wet or dry?
Check again, then tip both out on newspaper and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. On day 3, draw what the soil looked like when you tipped each pot out.
experiments.context: In this three-day experiment you find out whether a blanket of dry leaves keeps soil wet for longer, so plants need less watering.

flow.do: 1. Fill both pots with soil, pressed down the same. 2. Pour half a mug of water into each, slowly. 3. Cover the soil in one pot with a layer of dry leaves about 2 cm thick. 4. Put both in the same sunny spot.
flow.say: Both pots get the same soil and the same water. Only one gets a leaf blanket. Which do you think will stay wet longer, and why?
flow.kid: Fill both pots. Water both the same. Cover one with dry leaves. Put both in the sun. Which will stay wet? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Blanket test. You set up two pots of wet soil, one covered with dry leaves.

flow.do: The next day, feel the top of the bare soil. Lift the leaves and feel the top of the covered soil. Then push a finger 2 cm into each.
flow.say: Feel the top of each. Then push your finger in, about as deep as your fingernail is long, twice. Wet or dry?
flow.kid: Feel the top of each pot. Push a finger in. Wet or dry?

flow.do: On day 3, check again. Then tip both pots out onto newspaper and look at the soil inside.
flow.say: Let's tip them out. Which soil is darker? Darker soil is wetter. What did the leaves do?
flow.kid: Tip both pots out. Which soil is darker and wetter? Why?

check.q: Farhan, a boy in Hyderabad, covered one pot with dry leaves. After 3 sunny days, that soil was still damp, and the bare soil was dry and pale. Why?
options: The leaves added water to the soil
The leaves shaded the soil and kept the moving air off it, so less water evaporated
check.why: Water leaves soil mostly by evaporating from the top, faster in sun and wind. The leaf blanket shades the soil and keeps moving air off it, so less water evaporates. Farmers call a cover like this mulch.

flow.parent: In hot sun, the bare soil usually turns pale and hard on top by day 2 or 3, while the soil under the leaves stays dark. In very humid weather the difference is smaller, so give it an extra day.

activities.title: Shake the Mud: which bits sink first?

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle with a cap, about 1 litre
3 spoons of soil from a plant pot, with a few small stones and some sand if you have them
water

activities.safety: Close the cap tightly before shaking. Wash your hands after touching soil.

schedule.what: Shake soil and water in a bottle, then watch what sinks first and what stays.

activities.record: Draw the bottle after 5 minutes. Label each layer, and the cloudy water on top.
activities.context: This short activity opens the unit. You shake soil in a bottle of water and watch what sinks first, what sinks later, and what stays floating.

flow.do: 1. Put the soil in the bottle. 2. Fill it three-quarters with water. 3. Close the cap tightly and shake hard for 20 seconds. 4. Stand it on the table.
flow.say: Let's shake it up and then watch very carefully. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Put the soil in the bottle. Add water. Close it tight. Shake hard! Now stand it up and watch.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shake the Mud. You shake soil and water in a bottle, then watch it settle.

flow.do: Watch together for a few minutes without moving the bottle. Ask what your child notices and what they wonder.
flow.say: What sank first? What is still floating? What do you wonder about?
flow.kid: What sank first? What is still floating? What do you wonder?

ask.q: What is still floating after 5 minutes?
good: Tiny bits that make it cloudy

flow.parent: Stones and sand drop in seconds and make layers. A finer layer of silt settles over a minute or two. The water above usually stays cloudy, because the clay bits are tiny. Don't explain why yet. Write down your child's questions.

flow.do: Ask for a guess about the cloudy part, and keep the bottle to look at later.
flow.say: Clay is heavier than water. So why is it still floating? We'll find out. Let's look again tonight.
flow.kid: Clay is heavier than water. Why is it still floating? Guess! Look again tonight.
flow.think: Will the cloudy water be clear by tomorrow morning?

activities.title: Rice Water for the Tulsi: a week of using water twice

materials.item: a bowl or vessel kept by the kitchen sink to catch rice and vegetable washing water
a mug to measure
a tally sheet stuck on the fridge
potted plants at home or on the balcony

activities.safety: Use only water from rinsing rice, dal and vegetables. Never use oily or soapy kitchen water for plants.

schedule.what: Put the bowl by the sink. Make the tally sheet.
Each day, pour the caught water on the plants and add a tally for each mug.
Count the mugs for the week and work out how many buckets that is.

activities.record: Keep a tally of mugs reused each day. At the end, add them up for the week.
activities.context: In this week-long activity your family catches the water from washing rice, dal and vegetables and uses it to water the plants. You count how much you saved.

flow.do: 1. Put a bowl next to the sink. 2. Tell the family: rice, dal and vegetable washing water goes in the bowl. 3. Make a tally sheet with 7 days.
flow.say: Every time someone washes rice or vegetables, that water goes in the bowl. The plants will drink it instead of fresh tap water.
flow.kid: Put a bowl by the sink. Rice and vegetable water goes in it. Make a tally sheet for 7 days.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rice Water for the Tulsi. You set up a bowl to catch kitchen water for the plants.

flow.do: Each day, pour the bowl on the plants one mug at a time. Add a tally mark for each mug.
flow.say: How many mugs did the plants get today?
flow.kid: Pour the bowl on the plants, one mug at a time. Make a tally for each mug.
flow.wait: Do this every day for a week.

flow.do: On day 7, count all the tallies. Count how many mugs fill your bucket, and work out how many buckets you saved.
flow.say: How many mugs did we reuse this week? How many buckets is that?
flow.kid: Count all the mugs. How many mugs fill a bucket? How many buckets did you save?

ask.q: Why is rice water good for plants, but kadai water is not?
good: Rice water has only starch and a little dust
Oil coats the soil and the roots

flow.parent: Rice-washing water is safe and slightly milky from starch. Pour it on the soil, not the leaves. Most families reuse 10 to 30 mugs a week, but count your own.

activities.title: The RO Bucket (if your home has an RO purifier)

materials.item: an RO water purifier at home
a bucket to put under the reject water pipe
a 1-litre bottle

activities.safety: A grown-up finds the reject pipe. Don't open or unplug the purifier.

schedule.what: Fill a 1-litre bottle from the RO, and catch the reject water at the same time. Measure the reject water.

activities.record: Write: drinking water made, reject water caught, and how many litres of reject water for each litre of drinking water.
activities.context: This activity is for homes with an RO water purifier. You measure how much water the purifier sends away while making one litre of drinking water.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up finds the thin reject pipe, which usually goes into the sink or the drain. 2. Put its end into an empty bucket.
flow.say: This purifier has two pipes coming out. One gives drinking water. The other sends some water away. Let's catch that water.
flow.kid: Find the two pipes with a grown-up. Put the reject pipe in a bucket.
flow.context: This is the first step of the RO Bucket. You catch the water that a home purifier sends away.

flow.do: Fill an empty 1-litre bottle from the purifier tap. Stop when it is full.
flow.say: Guess first. While we fill this one bottle, how much water will go into the bucket? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how much water goes in the bucket. Then fill the bottle from the purifier.

flow.do: Measure the reject water by filling the 1-litre bottle from the bucket, again and again. Then pour the reject water into the mopping bucket.
flow.say: How many litres were sent away for one litre of drinking water? What can this water do instead of going down the drain?
flow.kid: Measure the bucket water with the bottle. How many litres? What job can it do?

check.q: Divya's family RO sent away 3 litres while making 1 litre of drinking water. What is the best use for those 3 litres?
options: Mop the floor or flush the toilet
check.why: Reject water holds the salts the RO took out, so it is saltier than tap water. It is fine for mopping, washing the balcony or flushing. Used on plants every day, the salt builds up in the soil.

flow.parent: Many older home RO machines send away 2 to 3 litres for each litre made, and newer ones less. If your purifier makes water very slowly, measure for a shorter time and compare.

activities.title: The Seed That Clears Water

materials.item: 2 or 3 dried kataka seeds (thetran kottai or nirmali), from an Ayurvedic or naatu marundhu shop, or 4 dried seeds from an old drumstick pod
a clean stone or a mortar to crush them
two glasses of the same muddy water, made as in the Phitkari Test
a spoon

activities.safety: A grown-up crushes the seeds. Nobody eats the seeds or drinks the water.

schedule.what: Crush the seeds, stir the powder into one glass of muddy water, and compare with a plain glass after 30 minutes and after 2 hours.

activities.record: Draw both glasses after 30 minutes and after 2 hours. Write which seed you used.
activities.context: In this activity you try an old way of clearing water: a crushed seed, used in India and Africa long before water plants.

flow.do: 1. Peel off any husk or wings. 2. A grown-up crushes the seeds into a fine powder. 3. Mix the powder with one spoon of clean water to make a milky paste.
flow.say: People in Tamil Nadu used this seed to clear water from rivers and wells. Women in Sudan used drumstick seeds. Let's see if it works on our mud.
flow.kid: A grown-up crushes the seeds. Mix the powder with a spoon of water.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Seed That Clears Water. You crush a seed to make a paste for clearing muddy water.

flow.do: Stir the paste into one glass of muddy water for 30 seconds. Stir the other glass the same, with nothing added.
flow.say: Same mud, same stirring. Only the seed is different. Which will clear first?
flow.kid: Stir the paste into one glass. Stir the other glass the same. Then wait.

flow.do: Leave both still. Compare them at 30 minutes, and again 2 hours later if you can.
flow.say: Is the seed glass clearer? Is it as fast as the phitkari was?
flow.kid: Compare the glasses after 30 minutes. Which is clearer? Was the phitkari faster?
flow.parent: Seed powders usually work more slowly than phitkari and need the water to be quite muddy. If the difference is small at 30 minutes, look again after 2 hours. Fresh green drumstick seeds do not work well, so use dried ones.

ask.q: Why do you think people used seeds before phitkari was easy to buy?

activities.title: Water Walk Round the Building

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a grown-up to walk with

activities.safety: Walk with a grown-up. Don't climb onto the terrace or the tank. Look at pipes, don't touch motors or switches.

schedule.what: Walk round your building or school with a grown-up and note every place water is used, wasted or could be saved.

activities.record: Make a list with three columns: where, what we saw, and one idea to save water there.
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your building or school with a grown-up, looking for places where clean water is wasted.

flow.do: Before you go, ask your child where they think the building might waste water.
flow.say: Where do you think our building loses water? Let's make a guess list first.
flow.kid: Where do you think the building wastes water? Make a guess list.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Walk. You guess where your building wastes water, then go and look.

flow.do: Walk together. Look at the common taps, the garden hose and the car-wash area. Look for the tank's overflow pipe and wet patches on walls. Ask the watchman when the motor runs and if the tank ever overflows.
flow.say: Let's look for water running when nobody is using it. Wet walls and green moss can mean a hidden leak.
flow.kid: Walk with your grown-up. Look for running taps, leaks and wet walls. Ask the watchman about the tank.
flow.parent: In many buildings, the overhead tank overflows every day when the motor runs too long, and the water pours out of a pipe high up. A dripping common tap or a long-running hose are also common. Be polite with the watchman and other residents. You are noticing, not blaming.

flow.do: Back home, finish the list. Choose one idea and decide who to tell, such as the building secretary or the school office.
flow.say: Which idea would save the most water? Who can make it happen?
flow.kid: Which idea saves the most? Who could you tell?

ask.q: What could stop a tank from overflowing?
good: An alarm when it is full
A float switch that turns the motor off

activities.title: Where Does Our Used Water Go?

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and coloured pencils
a grown-up to help trace the drain pipes

activities.safety: Look at drains from a distance. Don't open manholes or touch drain water.

schedule.what: Follow the drain pipe from your sink out of the building, then draw where the used water goes next.

activities.record: A drawn map: sink, drain pipe, building sewer line, city sewer, treatment plant, river or lake.
activities.context: In this activity you follow your used water from the kitchen sink to where it goes after it leaves your building, and draw a map.

flow.do: 1. Look under the kitchen sink to see the pipe. 2. From a window or outside, find the pipe running down the building wall. 3. Find where it goes into the ground or a covered drain.
flow.say: The water from our sink doesn't vanish. Let's see where the pipe takes it.
flow.kid: Look at the pipe under the sink. Find the big pipe on the building wall. Where does it go?
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does Our Used Water Go. You follow your sink's pipe out of the building.

flow.do: Draw the map. After the building, the water goes into the city sewer. In many cities it then goes to a sewage treatment plant. After that it flows into a river, a lake or the sea.
flow.say: At a sewage treatment plant, tiny living beings eat most of the dirt in our used water. Then the water goes back to a river or lake. What should never go down our sink?
flow.kid: Draw the water's trip from your sink to the river or lake. What should never go down the sink?

check.q: Why should cooking oil never be poured down the sink?
options: It cools, sticks inside the pipes and blocks them, and it is hard for the treatment plant to clean
check.why: Oil cools and turns thick inside pipes and sewers, catching other dirt and blocking them. It is also hard to clean out at the plant. Wipe oily vessels with paper first and put the paper in the bin.

flow.parent: Not all used water in India reaches a treatment plant. In many places it flows straight into a canal or river. Your city corporation's website may say where your area's sewage goes.

materials.item: a chart paper and markers
a bucket and a mug
the results from the Plate Test and the Water Walk, if you did them

projects.safety: Any repair to a tap or flush is done by a grown-up or a plumber.

schedule.what: As a family, choose three changes to try for a week. Make a chart with a row for each change.
Each evening, tick the changes the family made and note any water caught or saved in mugs.
Add up the mugs saved. Decide which changes to keep for good.

projects.record: The family chart, with ticks for each day and mugs saved, and a short note on which change to keep.
projects.context: In this week-long project your family chooses three ways to save water, tries them every day, and counts what is saved.

flow.do: Hold a short family meeting. Your child suggests changes, and the family chooses three. For example: scrape plates first, catch cold shower water, and turn the tap off while brushing.
flow.say: You are the water scientist in this house. Which three changes should we try? Which do you think will save the most?
flow.kid: Hold a family meeting. Pick three ways to save water. Which will save the most?
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Family's Water-Saving Week. The family chooses three ways to save water and makes a chart.

flow.do: Each evening, your child asks each person and ticks the chart. Any water caught in a bucket is counted in mugs.
flow.say: Did we do all three today? How many mugs did we catch?
flow.kid: Ask everyone. Tick the chart. Count the mugs caught today.
flow.wait: Do this every evening for a week.

flow.do: On day 7, add up the mugs. Talk about which change was easy and which was hard. Decide which to keep.
flow.say: Which change saved most? Which was hardest to remember? Which should we keep?
flow.kid: Add up the mugs. Which change saved most? Which will you keep?

ask.q: Why is it easier to keep a change if everyone in the family agrees?

challenges.title: The Two-Step Water Cleaner
challenges.context: An engineering challenge. Combine settling and filtering to get the clearest water you can from a jug of muddy water.
challenges.problem: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, has one jug of very muddy water. Make it as clear as you can in 40 minutes, using phitkari, settling and a home filter. Nobody drinks it.
constraints: Use only things from home and a little phitkari.
You have 40 minutes, including waiting time.
Nobody drinks the water, however clear it looks.
materials: a jug of muddy water made with red soil or multani mitti
a plastic bottle cut in half by a grown-up
clean cotton cloth, cotton wool, washed sand and small washed stones
two clear glasses and a paper with a big word written on it
general: Rub phitkari in the jug, wait 20 minutes for the flocs to settle, then gently pour the clear top water into a glass.
Make a bottle filter: turn the top half of a bottle upside down into the bottom half, then fill it with cotton wool, washed sand, then small stones.
Pour the settled water through the filter, so it catches any flocs that floated up.
creative: Filter first, then add phitkari, and compare with doing it the other way round.
Pour off the top water with a ladle, slowly, so the mud on the bottom is not stirred up.
Wash the sand well first. Unwashed sand adds its own fine dust to the water.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own two-step cleaner. Draw it, try it, and test the clearness with the word test. Then say what your cleaner cannot take out.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the muddy jug. Plan the order of your two steps.
flow.say: Which do you think works best: phitkari first, then filter, or filter first? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the muddy water. Plan your two steps. Which goes first? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two-Step Water Cleaner challenge. You plan how to clear a jug of muddy water.

flow.do: Build the filter and try your plan. Use the word test on the result.
flow.say: Can you read the word through your water? What could make it even clearer?
flow.kid: Build your filter. Try your plan. Can you read the word through the water?
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Phitkari first, then settling, then filtering usually gives the clearest water, because the filter doesn't clog with mud.

flow.do: Compare with someone else's way, or with a plain filter without phitkari. Then talk about what is still in the water.
flow.say: Your water is clear. Is it safe to drink? What else would we need to do?
flow.kid: Is your clear water safe to drink? What else is needed?

check.q: Kavya's water is now very clear. What must she still do before anyone could drink it?
options: Boil it or purify it, to kill germs
check.why: Phitkari, settling and sand make water clear, but many germs are too small to be caught. Boiling for a minute or a good purifier kills them.

challenges.title: The Tank-Full Alarm
challenges.context: An engineering challenge. Many buildings waste water every day because the overhead tank overflows. Design a model alarm that warns you when a tank is nearly full.
challenges.problem: Ammu, a girl in Kochi, sees water pouring from her building's tank every morning. Make a model tank from a bottle, and build something that shows a signal when the water is nearly at the top.
constraints: No electricity from the wall socket.
The signal must be easy to see or hear from a step away.
materials: a large plastic bottle with the top cut off by a grown-up, as the tank
a jug of water to fill it
a bottle cap, a cork or a piece of thermocol to float
a straw or a thin stick, tape, paper, string and a small bell or a steel spoon
general: Tape a stick to a floating cork. As the water rises, the stick pushes up a paper flag above the top of the bottle.
Mark a full line on the outside of the bottle so you can see the level.
Hang a bell on a string from a float, so the bell rings when the float lifts it.
creative: Real tanks often use a float switch. A float rises with the water and flips a switch that turns off the motor.
Put the flag where the person filling the tank can see it from far away.
Some buildings fit a pipe that lets the overflow fall into a lower sump instead of the drain.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own tank alarm. Draw it, build it, and fill your tank slowly from the jug. Does it warn you before the water spills?

flow.do: Fill the bottle tank slowly until it overflows into a tray. Talk about the problem.
flow.say: Imagine this is the tank on our terrace, and nobody can see inside it. How would we know when to stop the motor?
flow.kid: Fill the bottle until it spills. How could you know before it spills?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tank-Full Alarm challenge. First you see how a tank overflows when nobody can see inside.

flow.do: Draw two ideas. Build the best one. Test it by filling the tank from the jug, and improve it.
flow.say: Does the signal come before the water spills? How much warning does it give?
flow.kid: Draw two ideas. Build one. Fill the tank. Does it warn you in time?
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the bottle. A cork with a straw taped upright, sticking out through a paper bridge across the top, works well. The straw pushes up a paper flag as the cork rises.

flow.do: Talk about how this could help a real building.
flow.say: If every building had an alarm like this, what would change?
flow.kid: How could your alarm help a real building?

check.q: Why does a float rise when the tank fills?
options: The float is lighter than water for its size, so the water pushes it up
The float is pulled up by the lid
check.why: A cork or thermocol is much lighter than the same amount of water, so the water pushes it up and it stays on top. As the water rises, the float rises with it. A float switch uses this to turn off a motor.
