quiz.p: Meera, a girl in Class 3 in Tirunelveli, leaves a glass of muddy water on the table. The sand sinks at once, but the water stays cloudy for hours. Why?
opts: The tiny clay bits sink very, very slowly
The sand pushes the clay up
quiz.why: Clay is heavier than water, but its bits are so tiny that they sink very slowly. Picking 'sand pushes the clay up' guesses at a push that isn't there.

quiz.p: Why don't tiny clay bits in water stick together by themselves?
opts: They carry the same kind of electric charge, so they push each other apart
They are moving too fast to see
quiz.why: Things with the same kind of charge push each other away, like two balloons rubbed on hair. So the clay bits keep apart.

quiz.p: What does phitkari do in muddy water?
opts: It makes the tiny bits clump into flocs, which sink
It makes the mud float to the top
quiz.why: Phitkari makes the bits stick together into flocs, and flocs sink. It does not kill all germs, so the water still needs boiling.

quiz.p: In the Phitkari Test, glass A had no phitkari but was stirred too. Why?
opts: So the only difference between the glasses was the phitkari
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If both are stirred the same, any difference comes from the phitkari.

quiz.p: Which is the right order of steps at a city water plant?
quiz.why: Alum makes clumps, the clumps settle, sand catches finer bits, and chlorine kills the germs left.

quiz.p: What does the living layer on top of a slow sand filter do?
opts: Its tiny living beings eat many of the germs
quiz.why: The living layer is full of microbes who feed on germs and dirt. Much of the cleaning happens there.

quiz.p: A glass of well water is perfectly clear. Is it safe to drink?
opts: Not until it is boiled or purified, because germs are too small to see
No, clear water is never safe
quiz.why: Germs are invisible. Clear water still needs boiling, chlorine or a purifier to be safe. Picking 'never safe' goes too far: purified clear water is safe.

quiz.p: In the Plate Test, why did washing under a running tap use the most water?
opts: Water ran down the drain while the plate was being scrubbed
quiz.why: The tap poured out water that did no job while the plate was scrubbed.

quiz.p: Kavitha has four kinds of used water. Which one should go to her balcony plants?
opts: Oily water from washing a kadai
quiz.why: Rice-washing water has only a little starch and dust, which do not harm plants. The others harm the soil or carry germs.

quiz.p: Kavitha's RO purifier sends away reject water. What is the best job for it?
quiz.why: Reject water is salty, so it isn't good for drinking or for plants every day. It is fine for mopping or flushing.

quiz.p: In 1892, Altona had far less cholera than Hamburg, next door. What was different?
opts: Altona filtered its river water through sand
quiz.why: Both towns had the same air and ground. Altona's water passed through slow sand filters, and Hamburg's did not. This showed cholera travels in water.

quiz.p: Which of these saves the most water in a building where the terrace tank overflows every morning?
opts: An alarm or float switch so the motor stops when the tank is full
quiz.why: An overflowing tank pours away a lot of clean water every day. Stopping the motor in time saves all of it.

worksheets.title: Why Mud Sinks and How We Save Water (core)

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Madurai, shakes soil and water in a bottle and stands it on the table. Put these in the order they settle, first to last.
items.why: Bigger, heavier bits sink faster. Stones drop in a second, sand in a few seconds, silt over a minute or two, and the tiny clay bits can float for a day or more.

items.p: After the bottle settles, the water on top is still cloudy. What is making it cloudy?
items.why: The cloudiness is tiny clay bits. They are heavier than water but sink very slowly because they are so small. Salt dissolves and can't be seen, so it does not make water cloudy.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, says: 'If something is still floating in water, it must be lighter than water.' Is he right?
items.why: False. Clay is heavier than water, yet tiny clay bits stay floating for hours. Small bits sink so slowly that they look like they are floating. A strong answer gives clay as the example.

items.p: Phitkari makes tiny bits of mud stick together into soft clumps called ____.
items.why: Flocs are fluffy clumps of tiny dirt bits. They are big enough to sink, so the water above clears.

items.p: In the Phitkari Test, both glasses were stirred for 10 seconds. Why was it important to stir glass A as well, even though it had no phitkari?
items.a: So that the only difference between the glasses was the phitkari. Then any change in glass B must have come from the phitkari, not from the stirring.
items.why: A strong answer says this makes it a fair test: only one thing changes.

items.p: Revathi, a girl in Chennai, rubs phitkari in a glass of muddy water. After 30 minutes the water is clear on top, with brown mud at the bottom. Where did the mud go?
opts: It clumped together and sank to the bottom
items.why: The mud did not disappear. Phitkari made the tiny bits stick into flocs, and the flocs sank. All the mud is still in the glass, on the bottom.

items.p: Draw two glasses of the same muddy water 30 minutes after the Phitkari Test started: glass A without phitkari, glass B with phitkari. Show the clear water and the mud.
items.a: Glass A is cloudy all the way down. Glass B has clear water above and a brown layer of mud at the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference clearly and labels which glass had phitkari.
items.art: Two empty outlines of tall glasses labelled A and B.

items.p: Match each step a city water plant uses to its job.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each step catches what the step before missed. Clumping and settling remove most mud, sand catches finer bits, and chlorine kills germs.
pairs: makes tiny mud bits clump together
lets the clumps sink to the bottom
catches smaller bits in the gaps between grains
kills the germs that are left

items.p: Why does a city still add chlorine after the water has been through the sand filter?
opts: To make the water taste sweet
Some germs are too small to be caught by the sand
items.why: Sand catches mud and many germs, but not all. Chlorine kills the rest, and a little stays in the pipes to keep killing germs on the way to your home.

items.p: Water that looks clear is always safe to drink.
items.why: False. Germs are too small to see, so clear water can still make people ill. Drinking water must be boiled, chlorinated or purified. A strong answer explains why we can't trust our eyes here.

items.p: Sort each kind of used water: can it water plants, or should it go down the drain?
items.a: see items
items.why: Rice and vegetable water have only starch and a little dust. Oily, soapy-heavy and toilet water harm soil or carry germs, so they go down the drain.
items: oily water from washing a kadai

items.p: Lakshmi washed three plates in the Plate Test. Which way used the least water?
opts: Scrubbing with the tap off, then rinsing
Scraping first, washing in a bowl, rinsing with one mug
items.why: Scraping first removes most of the food without water. A bowl and one mug use only the water that does a job. A running tap pours water down the drain while you scrub.

items.p: Three of these save water at home. Which one wastes water?
items.a: Leaving the motor on until the tank overflows
items.why: The overflowing tank pours clean water out of the pipe and wastes it. The other three use less water or use it twice.
opts: Catching cold shower water in a bucket
Leaving the motor on until the tank overflows

items.p: Two cousins in Hyderabad argue about saving water.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason from the unit (for example, the mugs saved in the Plate Test, or the cost of cleaning and pumping water), and then fairly says what the other cousin has right.
items.why: There is truth on both sides. Farms do use most of India's water. But city water is cleaned and pumped at great cost, and it runs short in summer. Small savings in many homes add up.

views.says: Saving a few mugs at home is pointless. Farms use most of the water.
Our tap water was cleaned and pumped all the way here. Every mug counts, and if every family saves some, it adds up.

items.ask: Which cousin do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other cousin has right.

items.p: Your family has some RO reject water in a bucket. Name two good jobs for it, and say why it should not water plants every day.
items.a: Mopping, flushing the toilet, or washing the balcony or a scooter. It should not water plants every day because it is salty, and salt builds up in the soil.
items.why: A strong answer names two real jobs and explains the salt.

items.p: Using water again for a second job, like pouring rice water on plants, is called ____.
items.why: Reuse means using something again. Grey water, such as rice-washing water, can be reused for plants or mopping.

items.p: Two jars hold the same muddy water. Jar 1 has big sand grains. Jar 2 has fine clay. Both are made of rock. Which clears first?
opts: Jar 1, because bigger bits sink faster
items.why: Sand and clay are both heavier than water, but the bigger sand grains push through the water quickly. The tiny clay bits are slowed almost to a stop. Size decides how fast they sink.

items.p: Tiny clay bits all carry the same kind of electric charge. Explain how this stops them from clumping together and sinking.
items.a: Things with the same kind of charge push each other away. So the clay bits keep apart and never join into clumps big enough to sink.
items.why: A strong answer links 'same charge' to 'push apart', and 'apart' to 'too small to sink'.

items.p: Phitkari takes the mud out of the water.
items.why: False. Phitkari makes the mud clump and sink, but the mud is still in the vessel, lying on the bottom. You still have to pour the clear water off the top.

items.p: Nandini made the Phitkari Test with potting mix that was mostly cocopeat. The water stayed brown, even with phitkari. What is the best next step?
opts: Try again with red soil or multani mitti, which have lots of clay
items.why: Phitkari works best on clay. Cocopeat is plant fibre, and its brown colour is partly dissolved, so phitkari clears it less well. Testing again with a clay soil checks the idea fairly.

items.p: Label the parts of a slow sand filter, from top to bottom.
a: Living layer, full of tiny beings who eat germs
items.why: Water trickles down from the top. The living layer and the sand catch dirt and germs. Gravel holds the sand up, and clean water flows out at the bottom.
items: Living layer, full of tiny beings who eat germs
items.art: A cut-away tank with five blank labels from top to bottom.

items.p: A slow sand filter gets a slimy layer on top after a few weeks. What does this layer do?
opts: Nothing useful. It should be scraped off every day
Its tiny living beings eat many of the germs in the water
It stops any water getting through
items.why: The living layer, called schmutzdecke, is full of bacteria and other microbes. They feed on germs and dirt, so much of the cleaning happens there. Workers scrape it only every few weeks, when it clogs.

items.p: Put the steps of a city water plant in order.
a: Add alum so the mud clumps
Let the clumps settle in still tanks
items.why: Clumping must come before settling, and settling before sand, so the sand doesn't clog. Chlorine comes last before the pipes, so some stays to keep killing germs.
items: Add alum so the mud clumps
Let the clumps settle in still tanks

items.p: In the Leaf Blanket test, the soil under dry leaves stayed wet longer. Explain why, and say how this could save water on a balcony garden.
items.a: The leaves shaded the soil and kept wind off it, so less water evaporated from the top. Covering pots with dry leaves means you water them less often.
items.why: A strong answer names evaporation and links it to watering less.

items.p: Shreya's family RO made 1 litre of drinking water and sent away 3 litres. How much water did it use in total?
items.why: 1 litre of drinking water plus 3 litres of reject water is 4 litres in total. Only a quarter of the water became drinking water.

items.p: Sort each place where a home loses water: does it waste water while nobody is using it, or while someone is using it?
items.a: see items
items.why: Some waste happens with nobody around, like leaks and overflows. Fixing these saves water day and night. Other waste happens while we use water carelessly.
items: washing plates under a running tap

items.p: A family in Bengaluru has salty borewell water. They argue about buying an RO purifier.
items.a: A strong answer weighs both sides: salty water needs RO or another way to remove salt, but RO wastes water, so the reject water should be reused. It uses evidence from the unit.
items.why: Both views have a point. RO removes salts that boiling cannot, so it may be needed for salty water. But it throws away water, so a family with RO should reuse the reject water.

views.says: Our water is salty. Boiling doesn't remove salt. We need RO.
RO throws away three litres for every one we drink. In a city that is short of water, that is wrong.
Can't we have the RO and use the reject water for mopping?

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Give your reason. Then answer back from one of the other sides.

items.p: Draw a map of your home's used water: from the kitchen sink to where it ends up. Add arrows.
items.a: Sink, drain pipe, building drain, city sewer, sewage treatment plant (or a canal in some places), then a river, lake or the sea.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the water does not vanish, and marks where it gets cleaned, if it does.
items.art: A blank page with a small sink drawn in one corner.

items.p: Why do people in Chennai catch the cold water from the geyser pipe in a bucket while waiting for hot water?
opts: That water is clean and would otherwise go down the drain
The bucket makes the water hot
items.why: The cold water that comes before the hot water is perfectly clean. Catching it means it can water plants or flush the toilet instead of being wasted.

items.p: A blanket of dry leaves or husk on soil that keeps water from evaporating is called ____.
items.why: Farmers and gardeners use mulch so that plants need less watering.

items.p: Paati says, 'Clear water is ready for boiling. It is not ready for drinking.' What does she mean?
items.a: Phitkari and settling have made the water clear, but germs may still be in it. Boiling kills the germs. Only then is it safe to drink.
items.why: A strong answer separates clear (no mud) from safe (no germs).

items.p: The water used to rinse rice is good for watering potted plants.
items.why: True. It has only a little starch and dust, which do not harm the soil. Pour it on the soil, not the leaves.

items.p: A grain of sand drops to the bottom of a glass in a second. A clay bit can take a day. Both are made of rock. Explain why, in your own words.
items.a: The clay bit is far, far smaller. When something sinks, the water has to move out of its way, and that slows it. For a tiny bit, the water slows it almost to a stop. So size decides how fast it sinks, not only what it is made of.
items.why: A strong answer says the material is the same, so the difference must be size, and explains how water slows small things most.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Pune, says: 'If phitkari makes clumps, then more phitkari will always make bigger clumps and clearer water.' What is the best way to check?
opts: Test glasses of the same muddy water with a little, some, and a lot of phitkari, and compare
Add a whole lump to one glass
items.why: A fair test with different amounts, and everything else the same, shows what really happens. Water engineers do exactly this in a 'jar test' to find the right dose. More is not always better, and too much makes the water sour.

items.p: In 1892, Hamburg and Altona breathed the same air and stood on the same ground. Altona filtered its water, and Hamburg did not. Altona had far less cholera. What does this show, and why was it strong evidence?
items.a: It shows cholera spreads through water, and that filtering stops much of it. It is strong because the air and the ground were the same, so the only big difference was the water.
items.why: A strong answer sees that Hamburg and Altona were like a natural fair test, with the water as the one difference.

items.p: In 1892 two scientists argued about cholera.
items.a: A strong answer uses the Hamburg and Altona evidence to back Koch, then says fairly what Pettenkofer noticed: cholera was worse in some places and seasons, and not everyone who swallowed the germ fell very ill.
items.why: Koch was right that the germ in water causes cholera. Pettenkofer was right that not everyone who takes in the germ gets very ill, which depends on the body and on how many germs, but he was wrong that the germ alone could not spread it through water.

views.says: Cholera is caused by a germ that travels in dirty water. Filter the water and cholera falls.
The germ alone is not enough. The soil and the ground water of a place make cholera spread. I drank the germs and stayed mostly well.

items.ask: Which scientist does the Hamburg and Altona story support? Explain. Then say one thing the other scientist noticed that was true.

items.p: Label what each step of Kavya's Two-Step Water Cleaner removes.
a: Phitkari and settling: most of the mud, as flocs
Sand filter: flocs that floated up and finer bits
Neither step: germs and dissolved salt
items.why: Each step removes something different. Neither phitkari nor sand reliably removes germs or salt, which is why boiling or purifying is still needed.
items.art: A drawing of a jug with phitkari, an arrow to a bottle filter, and an arrow to a glass, each with a blank label.

items.p: A city's water plant has its settling tanks out of order for a day. What problem would the sand filters have?
opts: They would clog fast with mud and need cleaning very often
items.why: Settling takes out most mud before the sand. Without it, the sand gets all the mud and its gaps fill quickly, so water flows slowly and the filters need scraping much more often.

items.p: Tiny living beings in a sand filter and in a sewage plant eat dirt and germs. Should we think of them as workers, like the people at the plant? Give a reason.
items.a: A strong answer gives a reason, for example: yes, because they do much of the cleaning and the city depends on them, and they choose what to eat, or: they do it for their own life, not for us.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses what the unit says the microbes do, and is fair to the other view.

items.p: Muddy river water clears faster in a matka in the hot sun than on a cold night, if everything else is the same. Which is the best fair test to check this?
opts: Leave one matka in the sun and one in the cold, with the same water, the same phitkari and the same time
Use one matka and look at it twice
items.why: A fair test changes only the one thing you want to check, here the temperature, and keeps the water, the phitkari and the time the same.

items.p: Put these in order from the most water saved each day to the least, for a family whose terrace tank overflows for 10 minutes every morning, whose tap drips slowly, and who brush with the tap running for 1 minute.
a: Turning the tap off while brushing
items.why: An overflow pipe pours out far more water in 10 minutes than a tap does in 1 minute, and a slow drip loses the least each day. A strong answer explains the order by how fast the water flows and for how long.
items: Turning the tap off while brushing

items.p: Why is it a good idea to clear muddy water with phitkari before boiling it, even though boiling kills the germs?
items.a: Boiling kills germs but leaves the mud in the water. Clearing first takes out the mud, so the water tastes and looks better, and boiling and purifiers work better on clear water.
items.why: A strong answer says clearing and boiling do different jobs, and both are needed for muddy water.

items.p: About 97 out of every 100 litres of water on Earth are in the sea. Why can't cities just use sea water from the tap?
opts: It is salty, and taking the salt out costs a lot of energy
There is not enough of it
items.why: Sea water is salty, and people can't drink it or grow crops with it. Taking the salt out, as Chennai's desalination plants do, needs a lot of energy and money.

items.p: Design a home system that sends bath water to the toilet flush. Draw it with arrows and labels.
items.a: A drawing with a bucket or tank catching bath water, a filter or cloth to catch hair, and a pipe or bucket to the toilet, with labels.
items.why: A strong design catches the water, removes hair and soap scum, stores it only for a short time, and sends it to the flush. Grey water should not be stored for days, because it starts to smell.
items.art: An outline of a bathroom with a bucket, a drain and a toilet.

items.p: Water is used up when we use it, so one day it will all be gone.
items.why: False. Water goes round in the water cycle and is not used up. What runs short is clean fresh water in the right place at the right time, because cleaning and moving it takes work.

items.p: Which of these is the best evidence that the living layer on a slow sand filter does much of the cleaning?
opts: Just after it is scraped off, the filter lets more germs through until the layer grows back
items.why: If water gets less clean right after the layer is removed, and cleaner again as it grows back, that points to the layer doing the work. How a thing looks is not evidence of what it does.

items.p: Making tiny bits in water stick together into clumps, as phitkari does, is called ____.
items.why: Coagulation is the first step at most water plants. It turns tiny floating bits into flocs that settle.

items.p: Kamala Paati knew from her village that padikaram clears water. Appa thought it was only an old trick. How should we decide whether an old way of doing things works?
items.a: Test it fairly: try it and a control side by side, with only one difference, and look at the result. Old ways can be right or wrong, and a test shows which.
items.why: A strong answer says neither 'old' nor 'new' makes something right, and the test is what decides.

open_questions.q: What is the best low-cost way to make water safe for every family?
open_questions.why_open: Boiling uses fuel, chlorine tastes, and filters need care. Scientists are still testing which ways families keep using for years.

open_questions.q: Exactly which living beings in a slow sand filter do the most cleaning?
open_questions.why_open: The living layer holds thousands of kinds of microbes and tiny animals. Scientists are still finding out who does what, and how they work together.

open_questions.q: Do seeds like moringa and kataka clear water as well as alum, and are they safe to use every day?
open_questions.why_open: Tests show they work, but results vary with the seeds and the water. Scientists are still studying the best doses and long-term safety.

open_questions.q: How can cities stop losing so much water from leaking pipes?
open_questions.why_open: Many cities lose a large share of their cleaned water through leaks under the ground. Finding leaks without digging up roads is still hard.

open_questions.q: How much water will Indian cities have in 30 years?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on rain, groundwater, how cities grow and how much water people save. Forecasts differ a lot.

maths.problem: In the Plate Test, washing under a running tap used 8 mugs. Scraping first and using a bowl used 2 mugs. How many times as much water did the running tap use?
maths.explain: The running tap used 8 mugs and the bowl way used 2. 8 divided by 2 is 4. Check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. So the running tap used 4 times as much.
maths.context: This is about the Plate Test, where you washed three plates in three ways and caught all the water in mugs.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'a lot more' is vague. Dividing tells us exactly how many times more.

chart.title: Mugs of water to wash one plate

maths.problem: Your family washes 12 plates a day. Washing them the bowl way saves 6 mugs for each plate. One mug holds half a litre. How many litres does that save in a day?
maths.explain: 12 plates times 6 mugs is 72 mugs. Each mug is half a litre, so 72 mugs is 36 litres. That is about two or three buckets every day.
maths.context: This uses the Plate Test results to work out what a whole family could save in a day.
maths.why_maths: One plate saves only a little. Multiplying shows what it adds up to over a day.

maths.problem: In the Phitkari Test, the clear water on top of glass B was 0 cm at 5 minutes, 4 cm at 15 minutes and 8 cm at 30 minutes. Glass A stayed at 0 cm, then 1 cm at 30 minutes. Draw a bar chart for 30 minutes. How much more clear water did glass B have?
maths.explain: At 30 minutes, glass B had 8 cm of clear water and glass A had 1 cm. 8 minus 1 is 7. So glass B had 7 cm more clear water.
maths.context: This is about the Phitkari Test, where you measured the clear water on top of two glasses of muddy water.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which glass cleared more, and by how much.

chart.title: Clear water on top after 30 minutes

maths.problem: In the Phitkari Test, glass B had 4 cm of clear water at 15 minutes and 8 cm at 30 minutes. Arjun predicts it will have 16 cm at 60 minutes. His glass is only 10 cm tall. What is wrong with his prediction?
maths.answer: The clear water can't be taller than the glass. Once the flocs have all settled, the clear part stops growing, a little below the top of the mud layer.
maths.explain: Doubling worked from 15 to 30 minutes, but the pattern can't go on for ever. The glass is only 10 cm tall, and some of it is filled with mud at the bottom. So the clear part must stop at less than 10 cm.
maths.context: This is about the Phitkari Test, and about whether a pattern in your numbers can go on for ever.
maths.why_maths: Spotting when a pattern must stop is as important as spotting the pattern.

maths.problem: Divya's RO purifier sends away 3 litres for every 1 litre of drinking water. Her family drinks 8 litres a day. How much reject water is made each day, and how many 10-litre buckets of mopping water is that?
maths.answer: 24 litres a day, which is 2 full buckets and 4 litres more.
maths.explain: 8 litres of drinking water times 3 is 24 litres of reject water. A bucket holds 10 litres. 24 is 10 + 10 + 4. So that is 2 full buckets and 4 litres more.
maths.context: This is about the RO Bucket activity, where you measured the water a purifier sends away.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how small amounts at each fill become a lot of water in a day.

roots.context: We have learned why tiny mud bits stay floating, how phitkari makes them sink, and how a home can waste less clean water. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Without phitkari, your muddy water stayed cloudy for hours, though clay is heavier than water. Tiny clay bits sink very slowly, and their electric charges push them apart. Phitkari let them stick into clumps, and the clumps sank within half an hour. So whether dirt sinks depends on the size of its pieces, not only on what it is.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things into 'heavy things that sink' and 'light things that float', as if only the material decides. But the same clay floated as tiny bits and sank as clumps. How big the pieces are matters just as much.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Phitkari Test, glass A stayed cloudy for hours. Glass B, with the same clay and the same stirring, grew fluffy flocs that sank, and the water cleared in about half an hour. Nothing was taken out of glass B. The mud was all still there, on the bottom.

three.who_am_i: Your kidneys clean your blood all day, passing it through millions of tiny filters. You are a water cleaner too.
three.what_is_life: Tiny living beings in sand filters and sewage plants eat the germs and dirt in water. Whole cities depend on their work.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth has no new water. The same water goes round and round, and rocks, sand, sun and living beings keep cleaning it.

roots.thread: In muddy water, millions of clay bits each keep apart, because each carries the same charge. While they stay apart, none of them can sink, and the water stays cloudy. Phitkari cancels the charges, and the many bits join into a few big clumps. The clay is the same, and the water is the same. Only the way the bits are held together has changed, and the whole glass looks different.

teachings.teaching: Who can make muddy water clear? Let it be still, and it slowly becomes clear.
teachings.link: Stillness lets sand and silt settle, as in the shaken bottle. But your glass A showed that stillness alone is very slow for the tiniest clay bits. Phitkari helped them do in half an hour what stillness takes days to do.

teachings.source: Anguttara Nikaya 1.45–46, in the Pali Canon of the Buddha's teachings
teachings.teaching: In a muddy, stirred-up pool, a person on the bank cannot see the shells, the pebbles and the fish. In a clear, still pool, they can see them all. The Buddha said a stirred-up mind is like the muddy pool, and a settled mind like the clear one.
teachings.link: In the word test, you could not read the word through cloudy water, but once the mud settled you could read it clearly. The water was the same. What changed was what was floating in it.

teachings.source: Jain tradition: straining drinking water through a cloth, still done in many Jain homes
teachings.teaching: Many Jains strain their water through a clean cloth before using it, so that tiny living beings in it are not swallowed or harmed. The strained-out beings are returned to water like the water they came from.
teachings.link: A sand filter also catches tiny living beings, and some of them live on in the filter's living layer, cleaning the water for us.

science.text: Small particles sink far more slowly than large ones. Halve the size, and a particle sinks about four times more slowly.
Clay particles carry electric charges on their surfaces, and alum neutralises these so the particles clump.
Which of the thousands of microbes in a sand filter's living layer do most of the cleaning is still being studied.

other_view.view: Clay bits clump because of electric charges, and that is all. It is a useful fact for cleaning water, but it carries no lesson about people coming together. Reading lessons into mud says more about us than about the mud.

practice.title: Watch the water settle

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. Changes made: potting mix that is mostly cocopeat gives brown water that phitkari clears poorly, so the Phitkari Test asks for red soil, garden soil or multani mitti, which are clay-rich and stay cloudy for hours without phitkari. A peanut-sized lump swirled for 10 seconds, or a small pinch of powder, is enough for one glass. Flocs usually show within 5 minutes and the water is readable through within about 30. The step says what to do if nothing happens in 10 minutes. Clearness is measured with a word read through the glass and a ruler, so the child has numbers, not just an opinion. The Plate Test catches the water in a basin in the sink, and the measured water goes to the mop bucket, so the test itself wastes nothing. The Leaf Blanket test needs sunny weather. The step says to give it an extra day when it is humid. The RO activity is only for homes with RO, and a grown-up finds the reject pipe. The seed activity is optional, because kataka seeds must be bought and dried drumstick seeds are not in every home. The step says seeds work more slowly than phitkari. The building walk is done with a grown-up, without climbing to the tank. Both games work for one child alone. No test water is ever drunk. The spine (intro, Shake the Mud, the Phitkari Test, explanations, roots and quiz) fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1800s, many doctors believed cholera came from bad air rising from dirty ground. In Germany, the famous scientist Max von Pettenkofer said the cholera germ could not make people ill without the right kind of soil. So the city of Hamburg had not built filters for its drinking water. It pumped water straight from the river Elbe. Next door was the town of Altona. Altona took its water from the same river, further down, after Hamburg's sewage had flowed into it. But since 1859, Altona had passed its water through slow sand filters. In 1892 cholera struck Hamburg. About 8,600 people died in a few weeks. Altona, breathing the same air and standing on the same ground, had far fewer cases. On some streets along the border, homes on the Hamburg side fell ill, while homes across the road, on Altona's water, mostly did not. Robert Koch, who had found the cholera germ, used this to show that cholera travels in water. Pettenkofer even drank cholera germs to prove he was right. He got only a mild illness, but the evidence was against him. Hamburg built its own sand filters and opened them in 1893.
how_we_found_out.who: The people of Hamburg and Altona in Germany, the scientist Robert Koch, and Max von Pettenkofer, who disagreed
how_we_found_out.when: 1892, with Altona's sand filters working since 1859
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many doctors, led in Germany by Max von Pettenkofer, believed cholera needed bad air or the right soil, so clean drinking water did not matter much. Altona, with filtered water from the same river, stayed mostly safe next to Hamburg. That showed cholera spreads through water, and that filtering stops much of it.
